messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: QA Engineer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Uncertainty: Uncertainty, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Margaret

Margaret was seventy-three when she first sat down in the therapist's office, her posture rigid despite the soft chair. She had been referred by her primary care physician after months of insomnia and what Margaret herself called "being on high alert all the time." What brought her in now, after living with these feelings for decades, was a shift in her household: her husband had recently retired, and they were spending far more time together in their home in suburban Connecticut. The change had unsettled something in her that she could no longer manage alone.

The trauma that shaped Margaret's life occurred when she was eight years old. Her father, a man she had been taught to obey without question, had beaten her severely after she spilled juice on his newspaper. What Margaret remembered most vividly—what played in her mind like a film she could not stop watching—was the moment his hand came toward her, the sudden movement of his arm that made the room seem to tilt. She remembered his face, the sound of his breathing, the texture of the carpet against her cheek. These details arrived unbidden and in perfect clarity, as though she were standing in that room again rather than sitting safely at age seventy-three. Yet when she tried to speak about it in her own words, the language scattered. She knew what had happened, knew it in her bones, but the words themselves seemed to belong to someone else's story.

In the years that followed, Margaret had constructed a life of careful management. She became a quality assurance engineer—a profession that suited her temperament for order and control. At work, she could examine systems, identify failures, predict where things might go wrong. The work was methodical, and it kept her mind occupied. But over the decades, a pattern had calcified: she could not bear to be alone with men. Not because she feared violence in any logical sense—her husband was gentle, had never raised a hand to her—but because her body would not obey her mind's reassurances. When her husband entered a room where she was sitting, her shoulders would tense. If he moved too quickly, reaching for something on a shelf, her breath would catch and her muscles would coil as though preparing to flee. The hypervigilance was constant, exhausting. She found herself monitoring his every gesture, waiting for the shift in tone or posture that might signal danger. She knew, intellectually, that this made no sense. But knowing and feeling were two different things.

Funerals had become impossible. She had skipped her own brother's funeral five years ago, unable to face the combination of grief and the presence of male relatives in a confined space. The uncertainty of it—not knowing who would be there, what might happen, whether she could control her response—was unbearable. She had told her family she was ill. It was easier than explaining.

What troubled Margaret most, what kept her awake at night, was a guilt that had never softened. She had been a child, powerless, but she had come to believe that she should have done something. Should have fought harder, run faster, found some way to prevent what happened. That she had not done these things—that a child could not have done them—seemed irrelevant to the part of her that whispered, in the dark hours, that she had failed herself. She had also come to understand, much later, that her father had been someone she was supposed to trust. That betrayal, the fundamental wrongness of it, had never been fully metabolized. It lived in her as a kind of permanent uncertainty about safety itself.

Now, with her husband home every day, the walls of her carefully constructed routine were collapsing. She could not hide in the predictability of work. The uncertainty of unstructured time, the constant presence of a man in her home, the awareness that aging meant she was running out of time to make sense of any of this—all of it had finally pushed her to seek help. What she wanted, though she was almost afraid to say it aloud, was to feel safe in her own home. To look at her husband without her body bracing for impact. To attend a funeral and grieve without her mind fracturing into fragments of a seventy-year-old memory.
